1:
Why the writer signs himself Peter rather than Simon they explain alike. Gill notes the name is the same with Cephas, given at his conversion and respecting his after firmness; Henry adds it commended his faith and marked him an eminent pillar in the church. Robertson makes the choice deliberate: Paul always terms himself Paul and not Saul, and so Peter uses this name because he writes to Christians scattered over Asia Minor. He surveys how variously the apostles style themselves, Paul running from bare names in the Thessalonian letters to slave alone in Philippians and prisoner alone in Philemon, while John gives only the elder, close to the fellow-elder Peter uses of himself later here. Ellicott hears authority in the brevity: Paul constantly adds by the will of God to justify the title, whereas Peter need only mention it, his claim never having been questioned.

Two of them turn the modest title against a later claim. Gill observes that Peter does not style himself, as his pretended successor does, head of the church and Christ's vicar on earth, nor prince of the apostles, but only an apostle. Ellicott makes the same point from the article: Peter knows no higher title than the one he held in common with the other eleven, an Apostle and not the Apostle, neither bishop of bishops nor, which he says means the same thing, servant of servants. Yet Ellicott has a few lines earlier called the office a vicarship of Christ to the Church and not merely a representation of the Church Godwards, so that the phrase Gill refuses is one he has already used of the apostolate at large. He adds that Silas and Mark, though present, are not joined in the greeting, their support would have added little weight to the utterances of the Rock-Apostle.

Who the readers were is the oldest dispute here, and Barnes sets out the parties: some hold them native-born Jews converted, naming Eusebius, Jerome, Grotius, Beza, Mill and Cave; others that they were all of Gentile origin, naming Procopius, Cassiodorus and Wetstein. Ellicott is decided for the Jewish reading: the dispersion of Pontus means the dispersed Jews who live in Pontus, as the dispersion of the Greeks does in John, and the word rendered sojourners describes people resident for a time among strangers, as it might describe English people who have taken houses in Paris without becoming naturalised; so Palestine and not heaven is the home contrasted, Pontus and not earth the place of sojourn. Wesley agrees they were chiefly of Jewish extraction, long ago driven out of their own land, and notes that the five provinces are named in the order they occurred to a writer working from the east. Robertson takes the metaphor the other way, that heaven is our native country and we are only temporary sojourners here on earth.

On the word elect Robertson notes that it stands without the article and that Bigg would read it adjectivally, elect sojourners, and recalls the distinction between called and chosen. Calvin faces the practical difficulty, that election is hidden, so that while each is made sure of his own by the Spirit's testimony he can know nothing certain of others. His answer is that we are not curiously to inquire into our brethren's election but to regard their calling, counting as elect all admitted by faith into the church; that many fall away having nothing but the semblance is no objection, this being the judgment of charity and not of faith. He adds that Peter gathers their election from the effect rather than from God's hidden counsel, and turns on those who would make the merits of each foreseen, since Scripture everywhere sets the counsel of God against our merits. Clarke supplies geography instead, drawing on Lardner and Cave for Bethsaida, rebuilt by Philip the Tetrarch and named Julias after the daughter of Augustus.
2:
How far the word elect reaches divides them into four positions. Gill takes it at full strength: not to any office, nor of a nation, nor of a church, nor merely of effectual calling, but of eternal election both to grace and to glory, which he knew of them not by revelation but by a judgment of charity. Barnes grants the election and restricts the evidence: a man has reason to think himself elect just so far as he has evidence of being renewed by the Spirit and has holiness of heart and life, and no farther; no one can go up to heaven and inspect the book of life, nor depend on dreams or raptures. Ellicott refuses both the corporate evasion and the saving conclusion, holding that it is an evasion to say they were elect only in the mass, the election being individual and personal, and yet that for all their election they are not certain of salvation, the title implying no more than that God has put them into the visible Church.

Clarke takes the corporate sense outright and argues it from the letter's usefulness. If the apostle had directed his letter to persons elected to eternal life, he says with Lardner and Macknight, no one could have received it, since none could be sure of election that way till he arrived in heaven; they are called elect because, agreeably to God's original purpose discovered in the prophets, Jews and Gentiles indiscriminately were called to be the visible Church and entitled to all the privileges of the people of God on believing. He then transcribes at length the note of a fellow commentator whose own block stands further down the same page, saying that the Rev. J. Wesley has an excellent note here which he will copy out for readers who may not have his works at hand.

The note Clarke copies is a set-piece against predestination. Wesley begins by denying foreknowledge of God in the strict sense, since there is no more foreknowledge than afterknowledge with him, all things being present from eternity to eternity, the word being a condescension to our low capacities. Election in the scriptural sense he defines as God's doing anything in which our merit or power has no part, and the true predestination he reduces to three propositions, that he who believes shall be saved from the guilt and power of sin, that he who endures to the end shall be saved eternally, and that those who receive faith become sons; throughout which promise and duty go hand in hand, all being free gift, yet such a gift that the issue depends on our obedience to the heavenly call. Any other predestination he charges with cruel respect of persons, mere creature partiality and not infinite justice; with contradicting the universal offers of grace; with making probation meaningless; and with fatal consequence, all men being ready on slight grounds to fancy themselves of the elect number.

Robertson keeps to the words and finds the Trinity in them, Father, Spirit and Jesus Christ together in one clause. Foreknowledge he calls a late substantive occurring only twice in the New Testament, here and in Peter's sermon in the Acts, this epistle often preferring substantives to verbs. Sprinkling of the blood is used in the Greek Old Testament of the sacrifices but found in no non-biblical source known to him, and Paul does not mention this ritual use of Christ's blood though Jesus does, so it is unsurprising in Peter; Hort would see besides an ulterior reference to the blood of the martyrs, and Bigg says the whole epistle is a commentary on the three phrases of this verse. Ellicott arranges the same three clauses as origin, means and end, assigned to the three Persons respectively, and insists that foreknowledge implies not simply a perception of the future but the forming of a decision.
3:
The opening word is examined before the doxology is felt. Ellicott notes that this form of blessed is consecrated to God alone, wholly different from the happy of the Beatitudes and different again from the blessing pronounced on the Virgin, since this implies that praise is always due for something inherent in the person while that implies only that a blessing has been received. Gill guards it from misunderstanding: it is not an invoking or conferring of blessing, for there is none greater to be invoked and nothing can be added to his blessedness, but only creatures speaking well of him. Both he and Clarke record that the Syriac, Arabic and Ethiopic drop the connecting word, so that the clause reads blessed be God the Father, and Clarke would render it even the Father in any case. Ellicott adds that the address is no longer the Lord God of Israel but a nearer and tenderer relation.

On how God can be both God and Father to Christ, Henry and Wesley answer identically, that he is the God of Christ according to his human nature and his Father according to his divine. Calvin makes a rule of it: as God once marked himself off from fictitious gods by calling himself the God of Abraham, so now he wills to be known only in his Son, and those who form ideas of God in his naked majesty apart from Christ have an idol instead of the true God, as he says is the case with the Jews and the Turks; the mind that seeks God without thought of Christ will wander and be confused until it is wholly lost.

The verb draws the philologists. Robertson calls it a late and rare word found in the New Testament only here and at the end of the chapter, cites Bigg that the mystery religions probably borrowed it from Christianity rather than the reverse, and notes the Stoic use of the cognate noun. Barnes says the compound occurs nowhere else in the New Testament though it answers exactly to the Saviour's words to Nicodemus, and judges that begotten again would be the better rendering in every instance where the word occurs. Ellicott makes it carry everything: the being born from above, the fresh creation, the regeneration of Titus, the begotten of God of John's epistle, and in part the brought he us forth of James; the change is no metaphor but an act of creation parallel only to those of matter, of life and of humanity, since by it we are made partakers of the divine nature. His illustration is of an animal suddenly receiving the powers of a human being.

What the begetting refers to is disputed inside one block. Clarke reads it of the apostles themselves, whose confidence died with their Master and seemed buried in his grave, as the two on the road to Emmaus expressed it, and revived only with the certainty of the resurrection. Calvin reads it as a second creation, since we are born children of wrath and destined by nature to eternal death. But the editorial matter printed within Calvin's own block sides with Clarke against him, holding that the begetting seems not to refer to inward renovation but to what God did in raising Christ, to beget sometimes meaning to put one in a new state, as this day have I begotten thee constituted the Son a king. Ellicott forecloses the experiential reading: Peter speaks theologically and not phenomenally, of the begetting and not of the being born, of the resurrection itself and not of the preaching of it, and with God there is no interval between his begetting Christ from the dead and his begetting us thereby. He quotes Leighton that the resurrection is not the exemplar only but the efficient cause of the new birth.
4:
The three epithets are read as a description of a better Canaan. Ellicott says the notion is particularly Hebrew, that the Pontine dispersion had lost theirs in Palestine and have a better in store, and that the second word may mean the new Holy Land will never be profaned by Gentile incursions as the first was; the third, most poetical and found elsewhere only in the book of Wisdom, gives the unchanging beauty of a land where there is no winter. Calvin's editor reaches the same reading, that the inheritance cannot be destroyed by flood or fire, is not like Canaan its type which was defiled by its inhabitants, and is unfading as no worldly inheritance is. Clarke and Wesley take them morally instead: nothing impure can enter it, so its deterioration is impossible, and it is incapable of being enjoyed by any polluted soul.

Two of them pursue the last word into its history. Clarke derives the garden amaranth from it, a flower that keeps hue and odour long. Robertson notes the alliteration of the three privative adjectives and reports that the last is a rare word found on several tomb inscriptions, adding that those inscriptions will fade away though this inheritance will not, and will not be like a faded rose. Barnes separates the first and third: one denotes perpetuity against decay, the other perpetuity in the sense that everything keeps its original brightness, so that the crown of glory though worn for millions of ages will not be dimmed and the flowers on the banks of the river of life will be as fragrant as when first beheld. On the undefiled he quotes Benson's catalogue of estates got by poisoning, by murdering the right heir, by cheating helpless orphans and by grinding the faces of the poor.

Bengel's epigram travels through the catena three times. Ellicott quotes him that as the inheritance has been preserved so are the heirs guarded, neither failing the other; Robertson gives it shorter and names him; Wesley writes it unattributed as his own opening, the inheritance is reserved and the heirs are kept for it. Gill makes the guarding concrete: they are kept not in and by themselves, nor in the hands of angels, for no such trust does God put in them, but in the hands of Jesus Christ, out of which none can pluck them. Clarke supplies the military sense of the verb, a sentinel's word, and observes that on some frontiers posts are kept against irruptions and that heirs in their minority are kept in fortified places under guard.

Whether the keeping guarantees the end divides them. Barnes finds the perseverance of the saints taught here and argues for it oddly: the doctrine is desirable given human weakness, what is desirable may fairly be inferred true since God has made every arrangement really desirable, and no other security exists, since Adam fell and holy angels fell. Calvin says the contrary opinion, that we ought to doubt our final perseverance because we are uncertain of tomorrow, is a diabolical one prevailing under the Papacy. Ellicott is warier, fearing the words may give false assurance, since God can guard none of us without a corresponding exertion on our part; Clarke states the balance as no persevering without the power and no power without faith. On the salvation itself Ellicott refuses the bald sense of rescue from damnation, the perdition of the lost not entering the passage at all, and makes it deliverance from the trials of this life; Calvin means body as well as soul at the resurrection; Clarke reports some who understand the deliverance of Christians from the sack of Jerusalem, the end of the Jewish polity being the last time, and others the day of judgment; Robertson gives Hort's rendering, a season of extremity, and adds that Jesus said no one knows that day.
6:
A single relative pronoun occupies five of them. Robertson lists the candidates, the season just named, Christ, God, or the whole content of the preceding verses, and thinks the season probably right. Clarke sets out the same four and settles on the salvation now possessed. Ellicott says the last time is the first impression but prefers the whole complex sense of what precedes, quoting Leighton that they rejoice in being begotten again, in there being such an inheritance kept for them and they for it, and in nothing coming between though there be many deserts and mountains and seas in the way. Calvin refers it to their being kept by God's power and rejects both a future rendering and an imperative, since the next verses prove he speaks of present joy. Gill supplies the evidence Calvin is dismissing: the Vulgate and Syriac read that they shall rejoice, the Syriac adding for ever, and refer it to the last time.

That the same people exult and grieve at once seems inconsistent, and Calvin answers that the faithful know by experience how these coexist better than words express: they are not logs of wood, nor have they so divested themselves of human feeling but that they feel poverty as an evil and persecution as hard to bear; sorrow is so mitigated by faith that it gives place to joy, and joy, though it overcomes sorrow, does not end it. He distinguishes the godly from the reprobate not by the sorrow but by the willingness, the one bearing it as a tamed ox the yoke, the other as a ferocious horse into whose mouth the bit is forced, kicking and resisting all in vain. Clarke objects to the rendering heaviness, which can scarcely consist with rejoicing, whereas sorrow at something external and exultation in God are compatible; Wesley says the same shorter, that they were in sorrow but not in darkness.

On the qualifying clause they are unanimous in tone and divided in ground. Calvin takes the condition for a cause, since if God afflicted us without reason the bearing would be grievous. Barnes hears delicacy in it, the apostle suggesting the possibility rather than asserting the fact, as one would speak to a person greatly afflicted rather than tell him bluntly that he certainly needed this. Ellicott reads it as hope, that Peter will not take it for granted they must suffer. Wesley says flatly that it is not always needful. Clarke argues it from experience, that without trials men grow careless and in prosperity worldly-minded, and quotes a good man who said God could trust him with neither health nor money, and therefore he was both poor and afflicted.

Whether the tested thing is the process or the result splits them. Ellicott denies that the word means here what it means in James, where it is the active testing, and takes it as the attested worth, since one cannot compare a process with gold but can compare the character it brings out; it is not the faith but the faith's genuineness that is more valuable. Barnes takes the opposite, that the testing itself, and not the faith, is what is more precious than the trying of gold. Robertson holds the phrase identical with James and derived from there; Ellicott notes the same identity but suggests a common origin. Calvin observes that gold is tried twice, once to separate the dross and once to judge the purity, and is disposed to apply both to faith. The closing triad is distributed four ways: Ellicott assigns praise to word, honour to rank, glory to the admiration accorded; Henry makes honour the esteem, praise its expression, glory the lustre; Wesley gives praise from God, honour from men and angels, glory from the Judge; Clarke agrees but reserves the crowning to Christ.
8:
That the readers love a man they never saw is felt by two of them as biography. Ellicott hears a kind of tender pity in them, spoken by one who had himself seen so abundantly, and notes that the verb is the calm word of divinely given attachment, the one Christ used in questioning Peter by the lake and not the warmer word with which Peter answered him. Robertson thinks Peter has in mind the saying to Thomas, that those are happy who do not see and yet believe, and observes that Peter heard it in person, so could use it before John wrote his Gospel; Ellicott cites the same incident. Ellicott adds a variant, whom without knowing him ye love, which he judges inferior in sense and authority, and reports Bengel's remark that the clause is meant for a paradox, sight and knowledge being the usual parents of love.

Barnes defends the possibility at length: we may love a benefactor never beheld, such love is purest because least mixed with self-interest, and absence does not cool it, the ocean between us and a child not diminishing affection. He then defends faith itself by attacking the senses: the eye is subject to optical illusion, the ear to mistaken sounds, the touch to error about size, yet for practical purposes they serve; and we do not doubt the existence of London or Canton though we have never seen them, a merchant who refused to trade on that ground being reputed mad. Calvin comes at it otherwise, that the cause of love is faith and not the reverse, and that faith has eyes of its own which penetrate the invisible kingdom and are content with the mirror of the Word.

Both note what faith fastens on. Calvin denies that it lays hold on the bare name of Christ or his naked essence, or that it grasps God in the confused and implicit way the sophists prattle of, which would be to wander through devious paths; it regards what he is to us and what blessings he brings, since a man's heart follows his treasure. Ellicott claims Peter as at least as much the apostle of faith as Paul, faith here being the opposite of sight rather than of works, and suggests that the definition in the letter to the Hebrews may have been drawn from a study of Peter's writings. Clarke draws the practical consequence, that there is an equality between believers now and those who lived at the incarnation.

On the joy, Ellicott says the word for unspeakable seems coined by Peter, and Robertson calls it a late double compound found here only in the New Testament and otherwise in Dioscorides and Heliodorus. Full of glory is literally glorified, which Robertson likens to the glorified face of Moses and Calvin explains two ways, as magnificent or as solid against what is empty and fading; his editor paraphrases a joy anticipating that of the saints in glory, and Calvin adds that those not raised by it above the heavens boast their faith in vain. The last clause divides them over its tense. Calvin's editor says one must either render the participle as being about to receive or take it of the soul's present salvation, and prefers the latter; Barnes says their peace was such that they might be said to be saved already; Wesley makes it present outright, from all sin into all holiness, itself the pledge of the eternal. On the word souls, Gill notes that your is supplied, standing in the Syriac, Arabic and Ethiopic where the Vulgate has only the salvation of souls, and denies bodies are excluded; Ellicott rejects the reading that would take in other men's souls; Calvin asks why only souls when glory is promised the body, and answers that salvation is properly ascribed to what is immortal.
10:
The searching is taken as private rather than official, and one of them says so on another's authority. Ellicott quotes Calvin by name and with approval, that the inquiry refers not to the prophets' writings or teaching but to the private longing with which each was fired; Calvin's own block in this catena says exactly that, distinguishing what they taught from what they wished. Ellicott adds that the writings the Spirit impelled them to make were the text on which their longings were the comment, so that they laboured to understand what they had themselves written. Three reach for the same image: Henry says the words allude to miners who dig to the bottom and break through not only the earth but the rock to come at the ore, Wesley writes simply like miners searching after precious ore, and Clarke says they searched as after grains of gold hidden among sand or compacted with ore, which he claims is the force of the original. Robertson gives philology instead: the two verbs occur together in first Maccabees.

What they were searching for divides them four ways. Barnes takes the phrase to ask about a person, and lists against himself Bloomfield, Rosenmuller, Doddridge, Whitby, Benson and Grotius for time and Macknight for people, that is, what nation would put the Messiah to death. Ellicott reaches much the same, that they knew they spoke of a Messiah but longed to know who the man should be and at what period he would arise, so that they foresaw a Christ but could not foresee Jesus. Robertson keeps to time, that the prophets knew what they prophesied but not when it would be fulfilled. Gill alone thinks they got an answer: the coming was revealed as before the sceptre departed from Judah and before the second temple fell, and as four hundred and ninety years from a date given to Daniel.

Ellicott makes the passage the most striking in the New Testament on prophetic inspiration and sets it between two errors: the Montanist doctrine that every syllable is forced on an unconsenting man, which he illustrates from Montanus himself, that man is as a lyre and God as that which strikes the chords, the man unconscious and God alone awake; and those early opponents who held that Isaiah saw Mary and Jesus as plainly as we do. Between them he sets prophets who choose their own words yet feel a deeper meaning in them than they intended, and quotes Keble that as little children lisp and tell of heaven, so thoughts beyond their thoughts to those high bards were given.

Whether the verse proves the pre-existence of Christ is disputed flatly. Barnes says it is clear from the passage both that Christ existed before his incarnation and that the whole was arranged beforehand. Ellicott denies that it may be used so, since the title marks the office and not the person, and it is theologically incorrect to say the Anointed had any pre-existence except as a hope in Hebrew minds; he reads the phrase as the Messianic spirit, and refuses on the same ground the argument for the procession of the Spirit from the Son. Robertson stands with Barnes, that Peter definitely asserts the Spirit of the Messiah was in the prophets, and adds that the participle is neuter only by agreement and should be rendered he. Calvin says the ancient prophecies were dictated by Christ. On whose sufferings are meant, both Ellicott and Robertson give sufferings destined for Messiah, and Ellicott counts that eight of the ten times Peter uses the bare title it stands with suffering, while he never speaks of the sufferings of Jesus Christ. Calvin refuses to confine them to the head, since Peter does not separate Christ from his body and the cross has been from the beginning the way to victory; Ellicott calls that extension far-fetched.
12:
What the prophets were told is read as a limit, not an answer. Ellicott says the revelation was not sent in reply to their musings but occasioned them, and that its bounds are given: they were shown that they spoke for futurity, and no more, which he calls a sublime disappointment. Clarke agrees that God reserved the explanation of particulars to the time of fulfilment, and turns it against later writers: had interpreters of unaccomplished prophecy been content with the same information, we should have had fewer books and more wisdom. Ellicott and Barnes both deny that the prophets got no good of their own predictions. Calvin is sharper: the passage has been strangely perverted by fanatics so as to shut the fathers under the law out of salvation, when what it says is that they spread the table for others to feed on. Gill takes the revealed thing broadly, as covering the time, the age, the cruel sufferings and the glory after.

The serving image is in the Greek too. Ellicott notes that the verb is used of a servant bringing his master what he needs, commonly of serving a meal, so that the prophets wait upon us with the sufferings and glories of Messiah. He also prefers the reading unto you, and makes a habit of it: the first person plural is rare in this epistle where it might be expected, and where Paul puts himself on a footing with his readers, Peter utters his pastoral from above. He counts four places in the letter where Peter joins himself to his brethren, one a quotation and another a doubtful reading.

Ellicott then makes the verse a testimonial. Those who preached were the first bearers of the gospel to those parts, which he thinks shows Peter was not among them, half the churches perhaps looking to Paul as founder; so the Rock-Apostle sets his seal to his junior colleague, called in because these Jewish Christians were reacting against Paul's preaching. The participle for sent he would render sent once and for ever, and takes the clause as claiming for Paul the inspiration Peter received at Pentecost; the concurrence, he adds, refutes the Tubingen theory of divergence, except that the Tubingen school reject the epistle precisely because it makes the apostles too harmonious. Robertson quotes Bigg that the connexion between study and inspiration is a great mystery, and answers that this is no argument for obscurantism.

The last clause turns on a verb of stooping, and three describe the posture. Clarke has a man bringing a difficult writing into the light and bending over it; Ellicott has one standing beside a cave so as not to get in his own light and peering in sideways, a strained attention to what is caught out of the usual line of sight; Barnes has one drawing nearer to what he could not see at a distance. Whether the cherubim over the ark are meant divides them exactly: Clarke calls the allusion evident, Barnes reports it from Grotius but doubts it and doubts even that this was their posture, and Ellicott allows the symbol may have been intended without Peter's thinking of it. Ellicott explains what angels lack: not intelligence about the two natures, of which they know as much as we, but the capacity to understand flesh and blood with its temptations and its need of a Saviour; he points to Francia's painting, where two angels kneel by the weeping mother and the dead Christ without a trace of grief. Calvin answers otherwise, that things are open to us only as we see them in the mirror of the word, our knowledge not being called higher than theirs. Wesley makes the clause a gradation: prophets, righteous men and kings desired to see what Christ did, and what the Spirit taught of him the very angels long to know.
13:
All read the first clause as an eastern man tucking up a long robe, and each supplies the occupation. Henry has a traveller, a racer, a warrior and a labourer; Barnes has labour, a race or a conflict; Robertson has men in a hurry or starting a journey; Ellicott has dress let down for repose, and cites running in Kings and arguing in Job; Clarke adds that they girded themselves also when waiting on superiors at meals. Calvin agrees the figure is from that custom and rebukes those who philosophize more refinedly about the loins, as though lusts were meant to be restrained: they depart from the real meaning, for the words mean what Christ meant by girded loins and burning lamps, except that Peter doubles the metaphor by giving loins to the mind. Gill turns it against loose and vagrant thoughts: since angels desire to look into these mysteries, the readers should give themselves wholly to them.

An adverb divides them three ways. Barnes prefers the text's to the end over the margin's perfectly and takes it of not fainting under trial. Ellicott reads it strictly as hope perfectly, the point being that the hope should not be half-hearted, and quotes Leighton that it is perfect in continuance because perfect in its nature. Robertson reports that the Revised Version joins the adverb to the imperative but that Bigg, Hort and most moderns attach it to the participle before, so that it is being perfectly sober, not hoping perfectly. Ellicott presses a further nicety: the construction is not hope for the grace but hope upon it, as in the one other place where it occurs, so that the sense is to hope confidently on its strength.

The participle for brought is present, and three of them make the same use of it. Robertson says it pictures the process, that is being brought. Ellicott renders it a-bringing to you and quotes Leighton, that as the saints hasten toward that consummation it hastens toward them, every day bringing it nearer, so that all the malice of men and devils shall not cut them short of it. Calvin makes it an argument against sloth: there is no need to make a long journey to attain the grace of God, for God anticipates us and brings it to us, and how great then is our ingratitude if we neglect what is thus set before us. He also cites Pareus for the structure of the whole section, five reasons for sobriety and holiness drawn from their sonship, God's holiness, his impartiality, the price of their redemption and their new birth.

What the revelation is divides them further. Henry reports that some refer it to the last judgment but prefers the grace brought by the gospel, which brings life and immortality to light. Calvin sets out both, that the gospel reveals Christ, which Erasmus approves and he does not reject, and that a full revelation is deferred to the last day; he prefers the second, since Peter's object was to call us beyond the world, and when we look to that event the world is crucified to us. Barnes takes it simply of the coming to judgment. Clarke offers a fourth: if the allusion is to the judgment coming on the Jews, the grace may mean the believers' escape from Jerusalem when the Roman armies came. Wesley holds both ends at once, blessings to be brought at the final revelation and now brought by the revelation of Christ within. Ellicott notes what the change of wording implies: it is now the personal name and not the official title, since we no longer search to whom the title of Messiah belongs.
14:
The phrase is a Hebraism, children marked by obedience, as Robertson says, and Ellicott adds that children means relationship and not age, the figure running through the chapter from the begetting and the inheritance to the Father, the brethren and the begetting named again at its close. He notes that the usual characteristic of Jews in the New Testament is disobedience. Gill lets the clause look both ways, back to the hope they must go on holding and forward to the imitation required of children.

Being told not to be fashioned by their former lusts raises the question who these readers were, and two answer it differently. Ellicott concedes the force of the objection: the letter assumes its recipients had lived in ignorance and vice, and it is contended with much plausibility that this makes them Gentiles, since lusts of the flesh are not usually charged on Jews and the ignorance charged on them elsewhere has another tendency. He answers that such details weigh little against the opening verse and the tone of the whole letter, that ignorance naturally describes unregenerate Jews set against men who now know more than prophets or angels, that Jews were flesh and blood, and that the letter to the Hebrews assumes both ignorances needing atonement and many defiled by fleshly sin. Calvin meets the difficulty by another road: all knowledge without Christ is profitless, and the Jews, taught in a doctrine that was itself a true light, were blind in the midst of it while the Sun of Righteousness was hidden from them. He refuses the word its usual sense, the Platonic dogma that ignorance alone causes sin being false: the unbelieving may be reproved by conscience and still go astray as the blind.

Robertson notes that the verb belongs to outward pattern rather than inward form and occurs elsewhere only in Paul's charge not to be conformed to the world. Ellicott thinks Peter borrowed it there, and finds the sentence a little confused, the lusts standing as the model not to be copied where one would expect the readers' former selves. Barnes fills in what that self was: supremely selfish, living for gratification, indulging appetite so far as decency and health allowed, and aiming at wealth or fame. Clarke has the shortest form of the same thought: where we see the world's livery we see the world's servants. Wesley is shorter still, glossing the desires as those they had while ignorant of God.

Two correct the received rendering of the next clause. Ellicott says it should be after the Holy One who called you, and Robertson agrees that the preposition is a regular idiom set against the conforming just forbidden, so that God and not our lusts is the pattern. Barnes keeps the older sense but reaches the same doctrine by a general law, that men imitate the God they worship and rise no higher in virtue than he, so that from the character of a people's gods their own may be estimated. Clarke argues from the other side, that heathenism scarcely produced a god whose example was not abominable, the greatest being paragons of impurity, and that none of their philosophers could propose the objects of their adoration as objects of imitation. Ellicott quotes Leighton that the Hebrew word for holiness imports setting apart, so that it is sacrilege to apply to a profane use what God has consecrated; Calvin warns that the likeness is no proportion of equals but a direction in which to advance daily. On the quoted command Ellicott prefers the future reading, ye shall be holy, still a command and not a promise except that all God's commands are promises, and Robertson calls the future volitive; standing several times in Leviticus and addressed to all the people, Ellicott adds, it binds these readers twice, in the old Israel and the new.
17:
The conditional clause is taken by all as granted rather than doubted. Ellicott says the word casts no doubt but brings out the link between invoking such a Father and fear, and would paraphrase it, if you use the Lord's Prayer; the appeal is not merely to the Father but to the Father under that title, and the verb carries the forensic sense of lodging an appeal, so that whenever we appeal on the ground of his Fatherhood he decides the case without favour, allowing nothing for regenerate sonship and nothing at all for Hebrew descent. Gill takes calling on God to include the whole of worship, and adds that those who claim so near a relation must not cause that worthy name to be blasphemed. Calvin points to the blessing on Ephraim and Manasseh, where the name of Jacob was called on them that they might be counted his children.

Impartiality is explained three ways. Clarke argues it from God's self-sufficiency: all partiality among men springs from hope or fear, and God can feel neither, having nothing to hope or fear from any creature; he presses it hard, that a righteousness imputed and not possessed and practised will not avail where God judges by every man's work, and wishes those who fancy themselves safe in Christ's righteousness while impure would consider it. Calvin forestalls exactly that inference, denying that the words touch merit at all and calling it foolish and puerile to argue that because God judges by the integrity of the conscience rather than the outward appearance, salvation must be by works; faith, he says, is included in the work. Ellicott notes the singular: a man's work means all his conduct taken in the lump as one performance, good or bad on the whole. Wesley reads it as a life's tenor.

On the fear enjoined, Ellicott quotes Leighton that it is not cowardice but drowns all lower fears and begets fortitude, so that the righteous dare do anything but offend God, Moses being fearless before a proud king yet quaking when God appeared; he sets this against those who would make the word a timid attitude towards a hostile world. Henry pairs holy confidence in God as Father with awful fear of him as Judge, and observes that the fearless professor is defenceless while the desponding professor has no heart to use his advantages. Calvin opposes the fear to heedless security, which creeps in where there is hope of deceiving with impunity. Robertson notes that the word for sojourning gives us our parish, and that Peter is recurring to his opening address.

Whether the fathers' tradition is Jewish or Gentile is the sharpest question here, and it settles the older one. Barnes takes the vain manner of life as idolatry, the word being used of idols as nothing and unable to help, and the tradition as the sanction of venerated men of former generations. Ellicott argues from the word tradition, which in the New Testament means something sedulously taught and handed down as an heirloom, and so cannot describe a sensual life learned by example, whereas among the Jews it governed even how a cup was washed; he concludes the readers were certainly Jews by birth, then asks whether the Apostle of the Circumcision would dare call Judaism a vain manner of life and an Egyptian bondage, and answers from the council at Jerusalem, where Peter called it a yoke intolerable to the fathers themselves. Calvin answers differently: Christ granted the Jews knew whom they worshipped, and God always kept a small remnant, but the body of the nation had degenerated, so that Peter condemns the fathers' doctrine only as unconnected with Christ; thrice foolish, he adds, are the Papists who think the name of Fathers a sufficient defence of their superstitions. Clarke splits the difference, holding both nations wedded to inherited vanities; Robertson leans to Gentiles.
19:
Which lamb is meant divides them. Calvin says the similitude gathers up the ancient sacrifices but alludes especially to the Paschal lamb, finding the profit of reading the Law in comparing reality with type. Ellicott looks to Peter's own history: the first thing we know of him is the joining of two words, Messiah and Lamb, at the Baptist's cry, which he and John understood of the suffering servant in Isaiah rather than the passover. Robertson holds that both had that prophecy in mind, though the word is the paschal one. Ellicott repeats an earlier caution, that the word as makes sacrifice, like ransom, only a simile. Barnes, Robertson and Ellicott all take precious as costly rather than prized, Robertson observing that any man's blood is precious above gold, that of Jesus immeasurably more.

What was manifested splits Ellicott from Robertson outright. Robertson takes the participle of the Incarnation, set against the pre-existence just named. Ellicott denies that it means the visible life of the Incarnate Word at all, holding that the Messiah was pointed out as identical with the man Jesus, which was the Baptist's whole errand, and that the wording shows Peter had him consciously in mind. Ellicott finds in the times evidence that Peter thought the world's end near; Clarke takes the phrase of the Gospel dispensation, never to be succeeded by another, reports that some critics read the foundation of the world as the beginning of the Jewish state, and adds the rabbinic opinion that seven things existed before creation, the Messiah among them.

Foreordination raises the question of the Fall, and three answer at increasing length. Calvin puts the difficulty himself: since Adam did not fall before the world was created, how was Christ appointed Redeemer, a remedy being posterior to the disease; he answers from foreknowledge, that God foresaw man would not stand and provided a restoration to life before the first man fell into death, referring the curious to his Institutes. Ellicott draws the harder conclusion, that the Incarnation was no episode consequent on the Fall and that God had foreknown and predecided to allow the Fall itself. Barnes goes furthest, that creation must have had reference to this plan, and that it was more wise and benevolent to create the race with a certainty of apostasy than not to create it and leave the plan of salvation unknown to distant worlds.

The last clause turns on a reading and a question of persons. Ellicott prefers the better supported text, who through him are faithful towards God, and Robertson agrees the adjective is correct. Clarke supposes the clause refers to Gentiles, who never knew the true God till the preaching came; Ellicott meets the objection that Hebrews cannot be said to believe in God only through Christ from the warnings in the letter to the Hebrews against abandoning faith in a living God. Calvin makes the clause a definition of faith, since God is incomprehensible and faith could never reach him but for the Mediator: all knowledge of God without Christ is an abyss which swallows up our thoughts, as he says appears in Turks and Jews and in the Papists, who take the schools' axiom that God is the object of faith and speculate on hidden majesty with Christ overlooked, entangling themselves in astounding dotages. His second reason is that sin makes us dread every access, so that in Christ God in a manner makes himself little to accommodate our comprehension; and had Christ not risen, he says, God would still remain in heaven, yet Peter says he would not have been believed in. Wesley compresses that into a line: without Christ we should only dread God. Gill and Barnes keep to the exaltation as the ground of hope; Ellicott warns that we should terribly mistake the gospel if content to rest in Christ's love without accepting his revelation of the Father.
22:
The participle for purifying divides Calvin from Barnes sharply. Calvin says Erasmus badly renders it as a statement of what they had done, since Peter reminds them what they ought to do; and lest he seem to ascribe to us the power of purifying our souls he adds the Spirit: your souls are to be purified, but as you cannot do it, offer them to God. Barnes takes the opposite tack: the apostles were never afraid of human agency, no one is made pure without personal effort any more than one becomes learned without it, and the effort we make is usually the measure of our attainments. Gill holds both, ascribing the purity to the saints but not without Christ's blood and the Spirit's operations. Ellicott removes two words they expound: pure is no part of the text, and through the Spirit was a copyist's gloss.

The unfeigned love raises a suspicion in Ellicott: the epithet suggests that Peter was uneasy about the depth of their brotherly kindness, and he asks whether some coolness had arisen between the Jewish and Gentile members, so that the former needed reminding that they were truly brethren. He carries the reading into the next verse, where not of corruptible seed means not of Abraham's seed but of God's, the inheritance resting on regeneration and not descent, in which the Gentile converts are equals; Clarke puts it in a line, that being born of Abraham's seed will not avail. Calvin turns the love against the Papists, who weary themselves with invented superstitions while overlooking the chief thing God commends. Wesley reads the clause as a ladder, obedience and purity being freely bestowed so that they may go on to higher degrees of love.

What the incorruptible seed is divides them again, and here Calvin stands alone. Most commentators make the seed the word, he says, but the construction forbids it: the seed is the vital principle of grace, the restored image of God, and the word the instrument implanting it; the parable of the sower is a different figure, since there the seed falls on good or bad ground, while here bad ground is turned into good. Barnes and Ellicott take the word itself to be the seed sown, Ellicott adding that God creates afresh though men speak the creative word for him. On whether living and abiding describes God or the word, Barnes reports the critics about equally divided, names six of them for the word, and himself prefers God; Calvin prefers the word of the living God as less forced; Robertson says either makes sense.

The quotation from Isaiah is handled at very different depths. Gill notes that the mortality is not of wicked men only, as the Jews interpret it, but of prophets and preachers too. Henry contrasts a glory that fades like a flower with one that shines like an angel, and Barnes illustrates the verse from the speech of Wolsey on the frost that nips a man's root. Ellicott makes the citation an argument: the point lies in words Peter purposely omitted, that the Spirit of the Lord blows upon it and surely the people is grass, so that the withered flesh is the carnal Israel and the passage proclaims the equality of Jew and Gentile; Peter follows the Hebrew in saying all the glory thereof, and changes the word of our God into the word of the Lord, showing his readers that he held Jesus Christ to be our God. Calvin disputes the prophet's sense too, rejecting those who refer the fading flesh to the Assyrians or to Jewish confidence in human aid, since the prophet himself says the people is grass. Ellicott closes by making the peroration lead to the gospel of unity between Jew and Gentile as the supreme abiding revelation, and remarks that the Tubingen school may well wish to disprove the epistle.
